Short for Artificial General Intelligence: an AI system able to learn, reason and apply knowledge across a broad range of tasks and domains at or beyond human level.
AI built to act as an autonomous or semi-autonomous agent that interprets goals, plans actions, uses tools such as browsers, code or APIs, reacts to feedback and adapts to finish tasks.
Ensuring an AI system's goals and behavior match what people actually want, including their values, rules and intentions.
Standardized tests used to measure and compare how well AI systems handle specific tasks such as answering questions, recognizing images, writing code or following instructions.

The ability to work with AI productively and responsibly: knowing its strengths and limits, using tools effectively, judging outputs critically, acting ethically and adapting as the technology changes.
The field concerned with making AI systems behave reliably and avoid causing harm, even when they are powerful, widely deployed or in unexpected situations.
An integrated set of software, hardware and computing capabilities supporting the full AI lifecycle. The source page's definition is cut off after this point.
The end-to-end process of building, deploying and maintaining an AI system, from collecting data to making predictions, with stages like data preparation, training, testing and deployment.
A set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task, much like a recipe.
The situation where many organizations rely on the same or very similar AI programs, algorithms or training data.
A network of AI systems or agents that share information and coordinate their actions. The source page's definition is cut off after this point.
A term coined in 1955 by John McCarthy, Stanford's first AI faculty member, who described the field as the science and engineering of making intelligent machines.
A neural network method that lets a model concentrate on the most relevant parts of its input when producing an output.
Technology such as AI carrying out specific tasks according to explicit human instructions, where people define what to do and the system executes within set parameters.
The way neural networks learn from errors, by working backward through the network to find which parts contributed to the mistake.
Graphical models that use probabilities to represent cause-and-effect relationships among variables, like a map of how factors influence one another.
When an AI system produces results that favor or discriminate against certain groups of people.
Datasets so large that traditional data-processing software cannot analyze them, but which AI can mine for patterns and trends.
A computer program designed to simulate conversation with people, usually by text or voice.
Also called proprietary software: software whose code is restricted and not open for the public to view, modify or use.
A field of AI that lets computers see, identify and make sense of visual information from images and video.
The amount of input, such as text, an AI system can handle at one time while working on a task.
A machine learning technique where a model learns by comparing similar and dissimilar examples to grasp what makes things alike or different.
Artificially enlarging a training dataset by creating modified versions of existing data, without collecting new data.
Discovering patterns and trends in large datasets using statistical methods and machine learning.
An attack where an adversary deliberately inserts, alters or mislabels data in a model's training set. The source page's definition is cut off after this point.
A machine learning algorithm that predicts by asking a series of yes/no questions, splitting the data on different features until it reaches a conclusion.
A subset of machine learning that uses large multi-layer neural networks to automatically learn complex patterns from data.
Generative models that create new content such as images by adding and then removing noise.
Simplifying complex data by cutting down the number of variables while keeping the most important information.
Numerical representations that turn complex data such as words or images into vectors that capture their meaning or characteristics.
Techniques that combine multiple models, often called weak learners, to get a more accurate and robust prediction than any single model could give.
Designing, developing and deploying AI systems in line with human values, fairness, transparency and societal well-being.
AI programs that mimic the decision-making of human experts in a specific domain, using a knowledge base of facts and mostly if-then rules to reach conclusions.
Methods and techniques that make AI decisions and predictions understandable to humans rather than leaving them as opaque black boxes.
A machine learning approach where a model is trained across many decentralized devices or servers holding local data, without the data leaving its original location.
An approach where models learn to recognize or perform new tasks from only a small number of training examples.
Taking a pre-trained model and training it further on task-specific or domain-specific data. The source page's definition is cut off after this point.
Large AI models, often transformers, trained on vast and varied data so they can be adapted to many downstream tasks and serve as a base for many applications.
A highly capable, general-purpose AI model at or near the leading edge of AI development.
Also called GenAI: AI systems that can create new content such as text, images, music, code or video.
Generative Adversarial Networks: an architecture with two neural networks, a generator and a discriminator, that compete to produce realistic synthetic data.
A family of large language models that use the transformer architecture to generate human-like text from input prompts.
Graphics Processing Unit: a specialized chip originally built to render graphics by performing many calculations in parallel.
Cases where an AI system produces incorrect, misleading or entirely made-up information and presents it as fact.
An approach to AI that puts human needs, values and well-being first throughout development and deployment.
The ways in which people operate and engage with computer systems.
AI systems that include human feedback or intervention as part of how they operate.
A parameter whose value is set before a machine learning model's learning process begins.
A large technology company running vast networks of data centers that can rapidly scale computing, storage and cloud services to meet demand.
When a trained AI model makes predictions or decisions on new data it has not seen before.
The degree to which humans can understand how an AI system reaches its decisions or predictions.
k-Nearest Neighbors: a simple, intuitive machine learning algorithm used for classification and regression.
A technique in which a smaller, simpler model, the student, is trained to mimic the behavior and outputs of a larger one. The source page's definition is cut off after this point.
A structured database that represents information as a network of connected entities and the relationships between them.
An AI system trained on massive amounts of text so it can understand and generate human-like language.
A compressed, abstract representation in which high-dimensional data such as images, text or audio is encoded into a lower-dimensional space that captures its essential features and patterns.
The practice of managing the whole lifecycle of LLM-based applications in production.
Also called a cost or objective function: a mathematical measure of how wrong a model's predictions are compared with the correct values.
A branch of AI that lets computers learn patterns and make decisions from data without being explicitly programmed with rules.
A mathematical model of a sequence of events in which the probability of each next event depends only on the current state, not on how it was reached.
A set of practices combining machine learning, software engineering and DevOps to deploy, monitor and maintain ML models reliably in production.
A simplified mathematical or computational representation of a real-world system, process or relationship, used to make predictions or understand patterns.
The decline in a model's performance over time because real-world data has shifted away from the data it was trained on.
AI systems that can process, understand and generate several types of data at once, such as text, images, audio and video.
A branch of AI focused on enabling computers to understand, interpret and generate human language meaningfully.
A computational model inspired by the human brain, made of interconnected layers of artificial neurons that process and pass on information.
A method that helps a machine learning model improve by adjusting its settings so it makes fewer mistakes.
When a model memorizes its training data too closely, including errors and random quirks.
An AI model whose weights, source code, training data (or a detailed, auditable account of it) and development tools are available for others to download, run, inspect, reproduce, modify and improve.
An AI model whose core components are publicly released so anyone can download it.
Software whose original design, or blueprint, is made freely available for anyone to see and use.
An internal variable in a machine learning model that is learned and adjusted during training.
Using data, statistical methods and machine learning models to forecast future outcomes or trends.
Carefully crafting instructions, or prompts, to steer language models toward the outputs you want.
A security attack that uses malicious input to trick a large language model into behaving in unintended ways.
A technique that improves a language model's output by letting it look up external, up-to-date information before answering.
An AI system designed to solve complex problems by producing a logical, step-by-step chain of thought.
A type of machine learning in which an agent improves through trial and error by taking actions in a given environment.
The frameworks, principles and practices that guide the ethical and safe development and deployment of AI systems.
The field combining engineering and computer science, now often with AI, to design and build machines that perform physical tasks.
The ability to understand and reason about the three-dimensional physical world, including how objects relate, move and interact in space.
A training method in which a model teaches itself by creating its own puzzles from raw data and then solving them.
Understanding the meaning of language by examining the relationships among words, phrases and symbols.
Predictable mathematical relationships describing how AI model performance improves as model size, training data and computing power grow.
A machine learning approach where models are trained on labeled data: example inputs paired with the correct outputs.
Information generated by algorithms or simulations rather than collected from real-world events or observations.
A container for numbers organized in multiple dimensions, like a more advanced spreadsheet.
Breaking text into smaller units called tokens, which can be words, word parts or single characters, that language models can process.
Earlier approaches to AI that relied on explicitly programmed rules, logic and human-defined knowledge rather than learning from data.
The collection of examples, such as text, images or audio, used to teach machine learning models to perform specific tasks.
A technique where a model trained on one task is reused as the starting point for a different but related task.
A neural network architecture that uses attention to process and relate all parts of the input at once rather than sequentially.
Proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, a measure of whether a machine can show intelligent behavior indistinguishable from a human's.
A machine learning approach where models train on data with no labeled answers or predefined categories and must find patterns and structure themselves.
A specialized database built to store and efficiently search high-dimensional numerical representations (vectors) of data like text, images or audio.
An adaptation of the transformer architecture, originally made for language, to process and analyze images.
The numerical parameters in a neural network that set the strength of connections between artificial neurons and shape how the model processes information.
The ability of an AI model to perform tasks or recognize categories it was never explicitly trained on, using its general knowledge.
